title: Lesson 34: Data Model Design: Inheritance, Polymorphic Relationships, and Denormalization Tradeoffs
description: Three tools for records that stop being uniform: inheritance for kinds of a thing, polymorphic relationships for one field pointing at many things, and denormalization for paying write cost to make reads fast.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Data Model Design: Inheritance, Polymorphic Relationships, and Denormalization Tradeoffs”, a support escalation must attach to an Account, an Opportunity, or a Case, and all three roll up to an Account in this org’s model. What does the architect do?
options: Remove the polymorphism and give the escalation a normal lookup to the Account that every candidate parent already has, keeping the relationship reportable and securable.
Build a custom polymorphic field so one field can point at any of the three objects.
Create three separate escalation objects, one per parent type, so every relationship stays simple.
Store a parent type and a parent Id in two text fields, since custom objects get no polymorphic field.
questions.explanation: The lesson’s honest move is to dissolve the polymorphism into an existing hierarchy rather than import a free-form field that every report, query, and sharing decision has to branch on.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Record types can hide a field from the database, so subtypes that need genuinely different fields should always be record types.
A record that legitimately belongs to two subtypes should be assigned both record types.
Roll-up summaries work across lookups as well as master-detail relationships, so the relationship type does not constrain the model.
When subtypes share almost nothing, separate subtype objects tied to a shared supertype are cleaner than record types, and the cost is that one roll-up can no longer count across all of them.
questions.explanation: Record types cannot hide a field from the database, only from the user, so deep divergence calls for separate subtype objects behind a shared supertype, which is exactly why aggregation across them needs more structure.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Denormalization should be avoided entirely, because every stored copy is duplicated state.
A roll-up summary is platform-maintained denormalization that keeps the cached value current, but it requires a master-detail relationship and adds write cost on every child change.
A cross-object formula field stores its value and can be indexed, which makes it the faster option at high volume.
A hand-written trigger that maintains a count field is preferable because you control exactly when it updates.
questions.explanation: A roll-up summary gives a read without an aggregate query and the platform keeps the copies straight, at the price of a master-detail commitment, write cost on the parent, and a finite per-object budget.
